articles.body:
Tennessee Sen. Bill Hagerty (R) is projected to secure a second term in the upper chamber, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Hagerty, the former U.S. ambassador to Japan, defeated Democrat Marquita Bradshaw in a rematch. Bradshaw lost to Hagerty by nearly 30 percentage points in 2020. This year’s race was closer, with DDHQ reporting Hagerty at 52.66 percent over Bradshaw’s 45.73 percent with 81 percent of the ballots counted.

President Trump and key Tennessee Republicans, including Sen. Marsha Blackburn and Gov. Bill Lee, threw their support behind Hagerty. He was the favorite to win Tuesday.

A Democrat has not won a Senate seat in the Volunteer State since 1988.

Hagerty serves on the Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee as well as the Foreign Relations Committee, among others.

articles.title: GOP hopeful Eric Barlow wins Wyoming governor’s race
articles.summary: Wyoming state Sen. Eric Barlow (R) is projected to defeat Democrat Ken Casner and Constitution Party candidate Rebecca Bextel in the state’s gubernatorial race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Barlow, a former Speaker of the Wyoming House, will succeed term-limited Gov. Mark Gordon (R). DDHQ projected that Barlow beat Bextel by 48 percentage points…
articles.body:
Wyoming state Sen. Eric Barlow (R) is projected to defeat Democrat Ken Casner and Constitution Party candidate Rebecca Bextel in the state’s gubernatorial race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Barlow, a former Speaker of the Wyoming House, will succeed term-limited Gov. Mark Gordon (R).

DDHQ projected that Barlow beat Bextel by 48 percentage points with 20 percent of the vote counted as of 10:58 p.m. EST.

He won his party’s nomination in August, defeating a field that included state Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder, who was endorsed by President Trump, and Brent Bien, who was backed by the Wyoming Republican Party.

A veterinarian and rancher from Campbell County, Barlow won every county in the GOP primary despite facing opponents backed by Trump and party leadership in the Equality State.

Gordon endorsed Barlow in October, praising his experience in the state Legislature and willingness to work across party lines.

The GOP hopeful also received endorsements from former Wyoming Gov. Jim Geringer (R) and former state House Speaker Tom Lubnau (R).

Barlow focused his campaign on education, healthcare and water rights, including issues surrounding the Colorado River .

Casner, the Democratic nominee, campaigned on making elections more accessible and expanding opportunities for independent candidates to participate in the political process.

Bextel, who ran under the Constitution Party banner, criticized Barlow and Gordon, arguing that the state’s Republican leadership had failed to reduce the size of government. She proposed reviewing state agencies, freezing discretionary grants and reducing federal spending.

The race also highlighted divisions within Wyoming’s Republican Party, as Bextel received support from former state GOP Chair Frank Eathorne.

Wyoming has not elected a Democratic governor since Dave Freudenthal won reelection in 2006. DDHQ rated the contest as safe for Republicans ahead of Nov. 3.

images.caption: A sign on the border of Wyoming and Montana appears on the side of Belfry Highway, May 24, 2017, in Powell, Wyoming. Republican party officials in two Wyoming counties will meet on Saturday, Feb. 24, 2024, to begin awarding the first of the state’s 29 delegates to the Republican National Convention this summer, but the contest won’t resemble any other presidential vote held so far this year. The state is one of a handful to use a “caucus-convention” system. (AP Photo/Robert Yoon)

articles.title: Democrat ousts De La Cruz in key Texas House race, flipping battleground seat
articles.summary: Democrat and Tejano music star Bobby Pulido will defeat Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz in the race for Texas’s 15th Congressional District, Decision Desk HQ projects, a big win for Democrats in a key House battleground. Polling ahead of the race consistently showed Pulido in the lead despite the district’s Republican lean, with a…
articles.body:
Democrat and Tejano music star Bobby Pulido will defeat Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz in the race for Texas’s 15th Congressional District, Decision Desk HQ projects, a big win for Democrats in a key House battleground.

Polling ahead of the race consistently showed Pulido in the lead despite the district’s Republican lean , with a Texas Southern University poll in mid-October showing Pulido ahead 51 percent to De La Cruz’s 44 percent.

Pulido entered the race already well known by voters in the area — but not for his political experience. The Texas Democrat has a storied career as a Tejano music star with multiple Latin Grammy awards.

In a 2023 interview with The Hill, Pulido teased an entrance into politics ahead of his performance at the Congressional Hispanic Caucus Institute’s Awards Gala.

He drew national attention for his viral moments, frequently performing at his own rallies, and even offering to perform at quinceañeras and other events for families across the district. After a storied career as a musician, Pulido will now head to Congress.

He ousted De La Cruz, a two-term incumbent. De La Cruz was the first Republican to ever represent the 15th District since its creation, as Democrats have historically dominated politics in Texas’s Rio Grande Valley.

But South Texas shifted dramatically toward Republicans in recent years. While Democrats used to win the 15th easily, it swung hard to the GOP throughout the decade, with President Trump ultimately carrying it by nearly 20 points in 2024.

Pulido’s victory marks a rebound for Democrats among Latino voters in a district where they make up nearly 80 percent of residents.

Texas was ground zero for the mid-decade redistricting war of the midterm cycle. Republicans redrew five Democratic-held seats hoping to protect their House majority in 2026, three of them in South Texas. While the 15th was not one of the redrawn districts, Pulido’s race was one of Democrats’ few chances to strike back at attempted GOP gains.

Pulido will be sworn in on Jan. 3 along with the new Congress.

articles.title: Jacqui Irwin holds onto retiring Brownley’s House seat for Democrats
articles.summary: Democrat Jacqui Irwin (D), a state assemblymember, is projected to replace retiring Rep. Julia Brownley (D-Calif.) and lead California’s 26th Congressional District, according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Irwin defeated Republican Sam Gallucci in a district regarded as solidly Democrat, per nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report. DDHQ, The Hill’s election forecasting…
articles.body:
Democrat Jacqui Irwin (D), a state assemblymember, is projected to replace retiring Rep. Julia Brownley (D-Calif.) and lead California’s 26th Congressional District, according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Irwin defeated Republican Sam Gallucci in a district regarded as solidly Democrat, per nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report . DDHQ, The Hill’s election forecasting partner, predicted a safe win for Irwin in the days leading up to Election Day.

As the polls closed in California, DDHQ called the race for Irwin .

The 26th district covers much of Ventura County and part of Los Angeles County, home to several cities — including Moorpark, Camarillo, Thousand Oaks, Westlake Village and Oxnard —as well as part of Simi Valley.

The state legislator received endorsements from Brownley, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Los Angeles County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath (D) and California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) — who called Irwin a “trusted partner” in Sacramento.

Newsom praised her sponsorship of Proposition 1, a state ballot measure aiming to provide housing to homeless veterans, as well as her advocacy for stronger gun safety regulations and combatting climate change.

“Jacqui’s record of standing up for all of us and building coalitions to get things done gives her the experience and tools needed to represent us but also stand up to the Trump administration’s attack on our values and our democracy,” Brownley said in her endorsement.

Irwin entered politics in 2003, when she was appointed to the Thousand Oaks Planning Commission. She was elected mayor of the city in 2008.

In 2014, Irwin was elected to represent 44th State Assembly District and has served three terms since then. Her fourth term was as the lawmaker representing the 42nd State Assembly District in 2022 after redistricting.

images.caption: Assembly member Jacqui Irwin walks on the floor during an Assembly session at the Capitol on Aug. 31, 2026, in Sacramento, Calif.

articles.title: GOP New Jersey Rep. Van Drew loses to Democrat Zack Mullock
articles.summary: Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R-N.J.), who originally entered the House as a Democrat before President Trump’s first impeachment, lost to Democrat Zack Mullock in the race to lead New Jersey’s 2nd Congressional District, according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Mullock, the mayor of Cape May, won in a race that the Cook…
articles.body:
Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R-N.J.), who originally entered the House as a Democrat before President Trump’s first impeachment, lost to Democrat Zack Mullock in the race to lead New Jersey’s 2nd Congressional District, according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Mullock, the mayor of Cape May, won in a race that the Cook Political Report shifted from solidly Republican to likely Republican in the days before the midterm elections. Mullock led with 51.10 percent support compared to Van Drew’s 47.85 percent, DDHQ projected at 11:25 p.m. EST on Tuesday.

The Philadelphia Inquirer spotted Mullock thanking supporters after his win.

“I’ve already conceded about 10 minutes ago, I called Zack Mullock and I conceded his victory. He is and will be our new congressman for the next two years,” Van Drew told supporters after the election was called for Mullock, New Jersey-based ABC 6 Action News reported.

“I wish him the very best. I wish him success. His success is our success,” the Republican added.

Mullock ran to lead Cape May on a nonpartisan ticket, the “Community First” slate “because I’ve always believed in putting service to my community over allegiance to any one political party,” he said on his campaign website.

He campaigned on addressing concerns over the cost of living and addressing climate issues, as well as assuring that the U.S. lives up to its alliances forged during World War II.

“Both my grandfathers fought proudly against fascism and for our democratic allies in WWII,” he said on his campaign website. “They knew the extreme importance of the alliances formed and the peace and prosperity they have brought to our world.”

Van Drew was aiming to serve a fifth term in the House, having first been elected in 2018. The lawmaker was part of that midterm year’s “blue wave,” though he led Republican-leaning Cape May in the New Jersey state Assembly, according to the Cape May Star and Wave in 2007.

But in 2019, Van Drew changed his affiliation , joining the Republican Party after a New Jersey county party chairperson told him he would face political consequences if he did not vote in favor of impeaching Trump.

“It all boils down to that I may have my own individual opinion on one vote and that’s not going to be allowed, and I’m going to be punished for that, and that’s when I knew,” Van Drew told Fox News’s “Sunday Morning Futures” at the time.

images.caption: Rep. Jeff Van Drew, R-NJ., speaks during the Republican National Convention Tuesday, July 16, 2024, in Milwaukee. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya)

articles.title: Oregon Sen. Merkley wins reelection bid
articles.summary: Oregon Sen. Jeff Merkley (D) is projected to win reelection after a smooth race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s election partner. Merkley was leading Republican David Brock Smith by 21 percentage points — 59 percent to 38 percent — with 51 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 11 p.m.…
articles.body:
Oregon Sen. Jeff Merkley (D) is projected to win reelection after a smooth race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s election partner.

Merkley was leading Republican David Brock Smith by 21 percentage points — 59 percent to 38 percent — with 51 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 11 p.m. EST on Tuesday.

The incumbent senator was widely expected to be reelected to the safe Democratic seat he has held since 2009. Merkley, 70, was a state legislator and Speaker of the Oregon House for one term before being elected to the Senate.

In Congress, he has pushed for institutional reforms like streamlining the filibuster and banning congressional stock trading. He was the only senator to endorse Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) for president in 2016, and he has backed other progressive Democrats and ideas. Like Sanders, he has been critical of arms sales to Israel and Saudi Arabia.

In the current Congress, he is one of the top Democrats on the Senate Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee, where he has pushed for stricter regulations on Wall Street to protect the housing market and the banking system.

Merkley has also delivered record-breaking speeches on the Senate floor, including for more than 22 hours in October 2025, when he condemned President Trump for “authoritarianism” and “tyranny.”

National parties had largely stayed out of the race. Smith had only raised about $300,000 compared to Merkley’s $8 million.

images.caption: Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) speaks during the “People’s State of the Union” rally outside of the Capitol on Feb. 24, 2026, in Washington.

articles.title: MLB’s Teixeira wins Roy’s open Texas House seat
articles.summary: Former MLB first baseman Mark Teixeira (R) is projected to succeed Rep. Chip Roy (R) in representing Texas’s 21st Congressional District, according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Teixeira defeated Democratic opponent Kristin Hook in a race the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report has rated as solid Republican since February 2025. DDHQ…
articles.body:
Former MLB first baseman Mark Teixeira (R) is projected to succeed Rep. Chip Roy (R) in representing Texas’s 21st Congressional District, according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Teixeira defeated Democratic opponent Kristin Hook in a race the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report has rated as solid Republican since February 2025. DDHQ listed the former professional baseball player as safe to win the district, with a probability of winning consistently more than 90 percent since early June.

DDHQ projected Teixeira beat Hook by 7 percentage points , with 86 percent of votes cast as of 11:06 p.m. EST on Tuesday.

Roy opted not to seek reelection and instead run for Texas attorney general, but he lost the GOP primary to Texas state Sen. Mayes Middleton in the spring.

Teixeira received endorsements from Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) and President Trump. The former professional baseball player has shown support for Trump’s deportation agenda, writing, “ I stand with ICE ,” on social media after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents shot and killed Minneapolis resident Renee Good in January.

The president endorsed Teixeira on Truth Social in February, writing that the Texas Republican “was ‘loaded up’ with Accolades and WINS.”

“I know Mark well, and he is a TOTAL WINNER, on and off the field! … HE WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” Trump added.

Teixeira previously told The Hill that besides serving his constituents, entering Congress will bring him back to playing baseball again in 10 years.

“I’m definitely going to use this as an opportunity … you have 435 members in the House and another 100 senators, so you’re just not going to get a lot of one-on-one time,” Teixeira told The Hill in June, referring to playing in the annual Congressional Baseball Game. “This is an opportunity to be in a team situation, have fun, get to know guys and hopefully beat the Democrats.”

He played for the Texas Rangers, the Atlanta Braves, the Los Angeles Angels of Anaheim and the New York Yankees, where Teixeira won a World Series in 2009.

images.caption: Former Texas Rangers All-Star baseball player Mark Teixeira, who is running for Congress, makes a campaign stop in San Antonio on Feb. 13, 2026.

articles.title: Incumbent Tina Kotek wins Oregon governor’s race
articles.summary: Incumbent Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek (D) is projected to win the state’s gubernatorial race against Republican opponent Christine Drazan, according to nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ. Kotek, the state’s 39th governor who was elected in 2022 after she won a three-way contest against Drazan and independent Betsy Johnson, will be serving her second term as…
articles.body:
Incumbent Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek (D) is projected to win the state’s gubernatorial race against Republican opponent Christine Drazan, according to nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ .

Kotek, the state’s 39th governor who was elected in 2022 after she won a three-way contest against Drazan and independent Betsy Johnson, will be serving her second term as governor. She was one of the two first openly lesbian governors in the U.S., according to CBS News .

Earlier this year, the Democrat faced off against nine challengers and won the state’s Democratic primary by more than 80 points in her bid to secure the party’s nod.

Kotek, a former Speaker of the Oregon House of Representatives, narrowly won her first term against Drazan. Oregon has not had a Republican governor in four decades, and Kotek’s win will add another four years to the ongoing Democratic streak in the state.

The Cook Political Report in its latest rating shifted the race toward the Republican side, labeling it as “leans Democrat,” a shift from its previous rating of “likely Democrat.” The report noted that private GOP polling showed the race between the candidates was tied.

Kotek announced her gubernatorial bid in December last year, saying her decision to run for reelection was because “Oregon values are on the line,” according to local news station KOIN. In a move to pitch her bid, she said the “choice is between a governor who will stand up for Oregon and protect what we believe in, or a governor who will let Donald Trump do whatever he wants. I will always stand with Oregonians.”

About two weeks before the election, Kotek secured former President Obama’s endorsement, who said, “She will stand up to anyone if it means delivering for working families,” the Salem Statesman Journal reported . Obama had endorsed Kotek in her 2022 gubernatorial run.

“I am so honored to have President Obama’s support in this race,” Kotek said, according to the report. “Because of his leadership, Oregon has stronger healthcare, more ways to fight climate change, and expanded human rights protections. Thank you for helping our state make progress toward a better future for everyone.”

The incumbent governor has largely focused on issues of affordability, economic opportunity and education, according to her campaign website . She also pledged to stop data center developments until statewide standards are in place, support climate resiliency in communities and provide Oregonians ample access to reproductive healthcare.

images.caption: Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek (D) speaks at the State Library of Oregon in Salem, Jan. 31, 2023.

articles.title: Democrat Matt Little wins Minnesota House race to succeed Craig
articles.summary: Democrat Matt Little is projected to win Minnesota’s 2nd Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Little defeated Republican state Sen. Eric Pratt in the race to replace retiring Rep. Angie Craig (D-Minn.). Craig opted to run for Senate but ultimately lost the Democratic primary to Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan. The Democrat led his…
articles.body:
Democrat Matt Little is projected to win Minnesota’s 2nd Congressional District , according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Little defeated Republican state Sen. Eric Pratt in the race to replace retiring Rep. Angie Craig (D-Minn.). Craig opted to run for Senate but ultimately lost the Democratic primary to Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan.

The Democrat led his opponent 59.8 percent to 40.2 percent with 69 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 11:05 p.m. EST Tuesday.

Little’s win comes in a district that has steadily shifted left in recent elections, despite Republican efforts to make inroads with suburban voters in the North Star State.

The former state senator and Lakeville mayor ran on a progressive campaign, calling for “Medicare for All,” changes to federal immigration enforcement and a moratorium on new data centers .

He also took aim at President Trump’s handling of the Iran war, arguing the U.S. should withdraw from the conflict.

DDHQ’s preelection forecast showed Little with a 96 percent chance of winning, compared with Pratt’s 4 percent.

The Republican, a four-term state senator, sought to portray himself as an independent voice who could work across party lines. He emphasized lowering healthcare costs, cutting government waste and leaving decisions about data center development to local officials.

The two former legislative colleagues sparred during an October debate over health, Trump’s foreign policy moves and their records in the Minnesota Legislature.

images.caption: MORGAN, MN – AUGUST 2026: Matt Little answers a question during a Congressional Candidate Forum at Minnesota Farmfest in Morgan, Minn., on Tuesday, August 4, 2026. (Photo by Carlos Gonzalez/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images)

articles.title: Tommy Tuberville wins Alabama governor’s race
articles.summary: Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) is projected to defeat former Democratic Sen. Doug Jones in Alabama’s gubernatorial race, according to Decision Desk HQ. The two previously faced off in the 2020 Senate election, when Tuberville defeated Jones by roughly 20 percentage points, flipping the seat to Republican control. Tuberville will succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Kay Ivey,…
articles.body:
Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) is projected to defeat former Democratic Sen. Doug Jones in Alabama’s gubernatorial race, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The two previously faced off in the 2020 Senate election , when Tuberville defeated Jones by roughly 20 percentage points, flipping the seat to Republican control.

Tuberville will succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Kay Ivey, keeping the governor’s mansion in GOP hands.

The senator, a former college football coach, was first elected to the Senate in 2020. Before entering politics, he served as head football coach at Auburn University from 1999 to 2008.

Tuberville secured the Republican nomination in May with more than 85 percent of the vote, defeating Ken McFeeters and Will Santivasci. Jones won the Democratic primary with nearly 79 percent of the vote.

The Republican aligned himself closely with President Trump throughout his campaign, emphasizing immigration enforcement , tax cuts and conservative social policies.

Tuberville held a significant fundraising advantage heading into Election Day, raising approximately $17.7 million compared with Jones’s $6.8 million, according to an analysis of campaign finance reports through Oct. 27.

Alabama has not elected a Democratic governor since Don Siegelman won the office in 1998.

The race was marked by disagreements over Medicaid expansion and school choice. Tuberville opposed expanding Medicaid, arguing the state could not afford it, while Jones supported expansion and proposed phasing out Alabama’s CHOOSE Act school voucher program. Tuberville supported expanding the program.

Tuberville also declined to debate Jones, who held a campaign event in October featuring video clips of the Republican’s past statements.

images.caption: Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) speaks before President Trump arrives at a campaign rally at the Mitchell Center in Mobile, Ala., Oct. 2, 2026.

articles.title: Becerra wins California race to replace Newsom as governor
articles.summary: Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to win the race to replace Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) in California, according to Decision Desk HQ. Becerra, a former state attorney general, bested Republican former Fox News host Steve Hilton in the Golden State’s general election after leading in every poll since he notched first place in this summer’s…
articles.body:
Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to win the race to replace Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) in California, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Becerra, a former state attorney general, bested Republican former Fox News host Steve Hilton in the Golden State’s general election after leading in every poll since he notched first place in this summer’s top-two, nonpartisan primary.

California hasn’t elected a Republican statewide in two decades, but some in the GOP saw an opening as Democrats squabbled over who would replace Newsom as leader of the state that represents the world’s fourth-largest economy.

Former Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.) was seen as the front-runner earlier this year, but he exited the race and resigned from Congress amid sexual misconduct allegations. His departure helped clear a path for Becerra, who surged alongside Democratic billionaire Tom Steyer.

Steyer, who spent more than $200 million on his run, ended his campaign and endorsed Becerra after a third-place primary finish.

Becerra was boosted by his experience running statewide, his time in the Biden White House and his appeal to Latinos, who make up a significant portion of the state’s electorate. He’s now set to become California’s first Latino governor in more than a century.

The Democrat also sought to tie rival Hilton, a London-born former British Conservative Party adviser, to President Trump, whose approval rating has slipped even among Republican voters in the blue state.

Hilton pitched his campaign as a change to the status quo under Democratic leadership, hammering Becerra’s record as Health and Human Services secretary in the Biden administration, but he couldn’t scrounge up enough support to be truly competitive in Democrat-dominated California.

Becerra has big shoes to fill as Newsom, long floated as a potential presidential contender, exits the governor’s mansion. Under Newsom’s tenure, California has been a leader of Democratic states’ resistance to the Trump administration — and Becerra will be on the national stage as Trump enters the second half of his second term.

images.caption: California gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra speaks at a news conference on California’s housing affordability crisis in Long Beach, Calif., Sept. 4, 2026.

articles.title: Abbott concedes to Hinojosa in Texas
articles.summary: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) has conceded the governor’s race in Texas, clearing the path for Democrat Gina Hinojosa in the ruby red Lone Star State. Decision Desk HQ had yet to call the race as of 11:15 p.m. EST, but Hinojosa was leading by roughly 8 points with 80 percent of the vote in.…
articles.body:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) has conceded the governor’s race in Texas, clearing the path for Democrat Gina Hinojosa in the ruby red Lone Star State.

Decision Desk HQ had yet to call the race as of 11:15 p.m. EST, but Hinojosa was leading by roughly 8 points with 80 percent of the vote in.

“There are still votes to be counted, but mathematically, we’re not going to be able to win this election,” Abbott told supporters. “I let Gina know that I would assist her and her team in a period of transition.”

Hinojosa is set to flip the Texas governor’s mansion for the first time in more than 30 years, depriving Abbott, who was backed by President Trump, a fourth term.

The stunning gubernatorial flip comes as Democrat James Talarico was projected to win the Texas Senate race against state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R).

Major forecasters looked to the Texas Senate race as a toss-up in the closing days of the cycle, with Talarico expected to benefit from Paxton’s controversy-laden campaign. Hinojosa, on the other hand, was seen as having a tougher fight to oust Abbott, who had outspent her.

But Democratic momentum in Texas and across the country changed the tides on Tuesday, helping deliver the party control of both the Senate and the House, plus a series of key gubernatorial upsets.

Hinojosa’s Tuesday night win bucks the DDHQ polling average that had her slightly behind the incumbent heading into Election Day.

articles.title: Democrat Josh Turek flips Senate seat in Iowa
articles.summary: Democrat Josh Turek is projected to win the Iowa Senate race as his party closes in on a Senate majority, according to a projection by Decision Desk HQ. Turek defeated Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson in a close race to flip the seat vacated by retiring Sen. Joni Ernst (R). He notched just more than 51…
articles.body:
Democrat Josh Turek is projected to win the Iowa Senate race as his party closes in on a Senate majority, according to a projection by Decision Desk HQ.

Turek defeated Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson in a close race to flip the seat vacated by retiring Sen. Joni Ernst (R). He notched just more than 51 percent of the vote over Hinson’s 45 percent with 78 percent of the vote tallied at 11:20 p.m. EST.

The race had become quite competitive after Turek, a Paralympian gold medalist who pitched himself as a moderate Democrat, won the June primary . The national GOP and Democratic Party also poured money into the race as voters soured on President Trump and the war in Iran .

All the same, winning Iowa had seemed like a reach for Democrats throughout much of the year. It’s a state won relatively easily by Trump in three consecutive presidential elections, though the Hawkeye State was also won twice by former President Obama.

Turek’s victory follows stunning wins for Democrats in Texas and South Carolina, continuing a nightlong trend of his party’s Senate candidates winning big in red states.

Turek attacked Hinson over allegations that she increased her wealth while in Congress and emphasized her backing from Trump. The Hinson campaign targeted her opponent’s record of missing votes as a state legislator and tried to tie him to more progressive Democrats.

Hinson mostly leaned into her record supporting the president but highlighted times she had worked across the aisle in Congress. She was seen as a strong candidate in the race, in contrast to other GOP Senate candidates, such as Ken Paxton in Texas and Darline Graham in South Carolina, who had been seen as much more vulnerable.

That makes the win by Turek all the more impressive, while underscoring problems for GOP candidates in farm country hammered by high prices and tariffs.

Turek, 47, was born with spina bifida after his father was exposed to Agent Orange in Vietnam. He was a professional wheelchair basketball player in Europe and eventually competed on Team USA for four Paralympics.

He briefly worked for a company that provided mobility equipment and decided to run for the state House in 2022, winning by six votes a seat that had swung heavily for Trump two years earlier.

The moderate worked on healthcare and disability advocacy issues in the Iowa House and served on committees related to the environment and veterans’ affairs.

DDHQ rated the race as leaning in Republican’s favor ahead of Election Day.

images.caption: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Rep. Josh Turek speaks during a campaign rally, Nov. 1, 2026, in Council Bluffs, Iowa.

articles.title: Democrat Marni von Wilpert wins California race for Issa’s House seat
articles.summary: San Diego City Council member Marni von Wilpert (D) is projected to win the race for California’s 48th Congressional District and take the reins from outgoing Rep. Darrell Issa (R), according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). She defeated San Diego County Supervisor Jim Desmond (R) in a race where the district leaned Democratic, the nonpartisan…
articles.body:
San Diego City Council member Marni von Wilpert (D) is projected to win the race for California’s 48th Congressional District and take the reins from outgoing Rep. Darrell Issa (R), according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

She defeated San Diego County Supervisor Jim Desmond (R) in a race where the district leaned Democratic, the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report noted.

Von Wilpert led Desmond by nearly 19 percentage points with 64 percent of the vote reported, according to DDHQ as of 11:14 p.m. Tuesday.

She ran on addressing concerns over the cost of living, stronger restrictions on access to firearms and called for Immigration and Customs Enforcement to be held accountable. Von Wilpert also campaigned on helping reform the pathways to citizenship “for hardworking long-term residents and Dreamers who have grown up here as Americans,” her campaign website reads.

The California Democrat ran on protecting the rights of the LGBTQ community, herself being “a proud member,” according to her campaign website.

Earlier in her career, von Wilpert worked as a civil rights attorney and helped provide legal services to people diagnosed with HIV and AIDS through a free legal clinic in Mississippi, The San Diego Union-Tribune reported.

Von Wilpert was first elected to the San Diego City Council in 2020 and ran unopposed in 2024.

The district covers parts of San Diego and Riverside counties and includes the cities of Murrieta, Costa Mesa, Laguna Niguel and parts of Aliso Viejo and Santa Ana, among other cities.

This district has long been led by a Republican, with the exception of former Rep. Harley Rouda (D), who defeated former Rep. Dana Rohrabacher (R) in 2018.

Former Rep. Michelle Steel (R) reclaimed the district in 2020 before the congressional map was redrawn after the 2020 U.S. Census. Issa was elected to lead the district in 2022.

Issa announced in March that he would not seek reelection.

images.caption: Marni von Wilpert, a Democratic candidate for California’s 48th Congressional District, canvasses in a neighborhood on May 29, 2026, in San Marcos, Calif.

articles.title: Democrats win Senate majority

Victory in the Senate will deliver additional oversight powers to Democrats, who…
articles.body:
Democrats have won the Senate majority , a feat that seemed unreachable last year but that came to fruition with Republican candidates failing in states won just two years ago by President Trump, whose failing approval ratings was a huge drag on the GOP.

Victory in the Senate will deliver additional oversight powers to Democrats, who will now have a much bigger say on administration and judicial nominations.

They will also set the schedule for the Senate and have new powers to call in administration officials for hearings.

The string of Democratic victories sets the stage for Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to return as majority leader in 2027 and for hardball negotiations with Trump on an array of issues, including on federal spending levels.

It puts a significant crimp on Trump’s legislative powers and his ability to reshape the federal court system, though it will be necessary for Democrats to negotiate with the White House to win their own legislative victories.

Democrats needed to net at least four seats to win the Senate majority, which had seemed a tall order given the fact that most of the competitive seats held by Republicans were in states comfortably won by Trump.

But high gas prices elevated by the war in Iran along with more general worries about the economy gave Democrats ammunition to go after Trump and Republicans.

Senate Democrats flipped their first seat of the night in North Carolina when media election trackers declared former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) the victor over former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley.

Democrats got their next biggest call of election night when pediatrician Annie Andrews was declared the winner over Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), who had only been appointed to the seat in July after her brother, longtime Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), died suddenly.

Another big early call for Democrats came in Texas where state Rep. James Talarico (D) handily defeated state Attorney General Ken Paxton, whom Trump controversially endorsed over Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) in the GOP Senate primary.

The political headwinds facing Republican candidates grew steadily stronger amid the deeply unpopular Iran war. Earlier in the year, Trump also took political hits from the killings of two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis by federal immigration officers sent to the city by an administration focused on immigration.

Trump also launched a trade war that raised prices, including with Canada, one of America’s oldest allies. That became an issue in a number of states, including those along the long border with Canada.

Political handicappers initially gave Democrats well below 50-50 odds of winning back control of the upper chamber, but by the final week of campaigning before Election Day, they were favored to win control of both the Senate and House.

Decision Desk HQ in the final week of the campaign gave Democrats a 60 percent chance of winning back the upper chamber. On Tuesday at about 6 p.m. EST, the Kalshi prediction market put the odds at 76 percent.

The loss of the Senate is a pointed rebuke of Trump, who campaigned extensively for GOP candidates throughout October, including Sens. Jon Husted (Ohio), Dan Sullivan (Alaska), Roger Marshall (Kan.), Graham and Paxton.

Democrats winning control of the Senate leaves Trump’s agenda, even in the postelection lame-duck session of Congress, in limbo. They have warned that Trump’s judicial and executive branch nominees will have a difficult time getting confirmed in the Senate.

Now, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) must decide whether to spend much of the lame-duck session trying to confirm as many Trump nominees as possible or spend weeks working on a budget reconciliation package to fund the Defense Department over Democratic objections.

Schumer is expected to be easily elected as majority leader when Senate Democrats hold their leadership elections in early December, even though some senators-elect, such as Juliana Stratton in Illinois, have threatened not to support him.

Thune is expected to be elected as Senate minority leader when Republicans hold their leadership election next week.

The president campaigned in Rock Hill, S.C.; Chillicothe, Ohio; and Corpus Christi, Texas — among other battleground states — in the final week and predicted victory for Republicans, despite polls showing them down or tied even in GOP-leaning states.

Trump urged supporters to pretend he’s “on the ballot” in hopes of driving low-propensity Republican voters who turned out in big numbers in the 2024 election to the polls on Election Day.

Democrats in the Senate may now face pressure from their own base to turn their electoral victories into legislative wins, despite the reality that they will still need Trump’s signature to turn their bills into laws.

Democrats won big on election night despite being heavily outspent by Republican Party committees and aligned outside groups.

Senate Republicans and aligned super PACs spent significantly more than their Democratic counterparts, drowning Democratic candidates in negative attack ads.

In Texas, outside groups spent more than $153 million against Talarico, while in Ohio groups spent more than $115 million against former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), according to OpenSecrets.org, a group that tracks campaign fundraising.

In Michigan, GOP-aligned groups spent more than $91 million against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, and in Maine, they spent more than $55 million against Democratic nominee Troy Jackson.

A Republican source familiar with the Senate fundraising dynamics estimated that Thune and aligned outside groups spent nearly three-quarters of a billion dollars to protect the Senate majority.

Thune urged GOP colleagues to run on their legislative record in Washington, especially the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which made permanent Trump’s tax cuts from his first term, made permanent major tax breaks for corporations and included new tax break, such as “no tax on tips” and “no tax on overtime.”

Senate Democrats focused their campaign message on the issue of affordability and what they called a “culture of corruption” under Trump’s leadership in Washington.

Schumer warned colleagues last month that Democrats were being outspent in key races, describing the spending disparity as “one enormous advantage” for Republicans.

Democratic candidates made up for some of the Republicans overall fundraising advantage by raising more than their Republican opponents for their personal campaign coffers.

Democrats in more than a dozen Senate races raised more than $250 million during the third fundraising quarter of 2026 compared with more than $56 million collected by Republicans.

In Texas, Talarico raised more than $60 million, while Paxton raised about $10 million during that span.

In Ohio, Brown outraised Sen. John Husted (R) $23 million to $4.8 million from the start of July to the end of September.

In Alaska, former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) raised $17 million in the third quarter, while Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) raised just less than $3 million.

Voter dissatisfaction over rising prices, Trump’s handling of the economy, and the drawn-out military conflict with Iran, which they blamed for high gas and diesel prices, eclipsed the GOP fundraising advantage and message.

A Fox News poll of registered voters conducted nationwide in mid-October found that Trump’s job approval had sunk to 36 percent and that 64 percent of voters disapproved of his performance.

In a troubling sign for GOP candidates, only 22 percent of independents said they approved of Trump’s job performance.

The president’s job approval rating among Republicans dipped to 76 percent, according to the poll.

images.caption: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) takes questions from reporters after a weekly luncheon, at the Capitol, Sept. 15,, 2026, in Washington.

articles.title: Brown pulls off Senate comeback bid, beating Husted in Ohio
articles.summary: Former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) is projected to head back to the Senate, beating Sen. Jon Husted (R) in Ohio, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Just two years after Brown, a three-term senator, was ousted by Sen. Bernie Moreno (R) in a tough 2024 race, his comeback bid faced steep odds in the once-purple…
articles.body:
Former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) is projected to head back to the Senate, beating Sen. Jon Husted (R) in Ohio, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Just two years after Brown, a three-term senator, was ousted by Sen. Bernie Moreno (R) in a tough 2024 race, his comeback bid faced steep odds in the once-purple state that has become increasingly red in the President Trump era.

Brown prevailed Tuesday after polls showed him narrowly leading Husted, who was backed by Trump, against the backdrop of a promising midterm landscape for Democrats across the country.

DDHQ reported a tight race between them, one of the tighter of the night, but with Brown ahead of Husted by just more than 2 points with 83 percent of the ballots counted, projecting he would pull out the win.

DDHQ’s polling averages showed Brown ahead by 3 points in the week before the election as major forecasters rated it a toss-up.

Tuesday’s contest was a special election to fill the remainder of Vice President Vance’s term in the Senate, which was cut short when he ascended to the White House. Last year, Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) appointed Husted , who was then the lieutenant governor, to temporarily fill the open seat.

With his midterm win, Brown will take over the Senate seat until the next cycle but will need to run again in 2028 if he wants to secure a full, six-year term.

Brown, a rare Democrat to see statewide success in Ohio, was a major recruit for his party as it sought to capitalize on voter frustration with Trump.

A strong fundraiser, he brought in $23.1 million to Husted’s $5 million in the third quarter alone, which helped him overcome significant Republican money spent against him.

The GOP-aligned Senate Leadership Fund, the Trump-backed MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk’s America PAC all poured in for a reported total of $113.5 million attacking Brown, according to the Ohio Capital Journal, compared with $69.5 million in outside groups spending to attack Husted.

The Senate race in Ohio smashed records with more than $500 million in ad spending this cycle, according to AdImpact data.

The tight contest had also brought Trump and former President Obama to the state as they rallied around the Senate contest and a highly competitive fight for the governor’s mansion between Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat Amy Acton.

images.caption: Democratic Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown speaks during a campaign rally, Oct. 24, 2026, in Cleveland.

articles.title: Poindexter topples Miller in Ohio amid scandal
articles.summary: Democrats scored an upset victory in Ohio as Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker, defeated two-term Republican Rep. Max Miller in the 7th District encompassing the southern suburbs of Cleveland, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projects. Poindexter led Miller by nearly 8 percentage points with 67 percent of the vote reported as of 11:16 p.m. Tuesday, according…
articles.body:
Democrats scored an upset victory in Ohio as Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker, defeated two-term Republican Rep. Max Miller in the 7th District encompassing the southern suburbs of Cleveland, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projects .

Poindexter led Miller by nearly 8 percentage points with 67 percent of the vote reported as of 11:16 p.m. Tuesday, according to DDHQ.

The race was not initially expected to be close. The district has been traditionally conservative, and President Trump won there by 11 percentage points in 2024.

But Miller was embroiled in a very public family feud that erupted late in the campaign, featuring explosive allegations by his ex-wife that Miller had violently abused her and their young daughter. Miller’s former father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), said Miller lacks the character to serve in Congress and instead should “seek professional help.”

“He is a danger to my daughter, and I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter,” Moreno said in August.

Miller has denied the allegations, accusing his ex-wife of being mentally ill and inventing the abuse allegations merely to win custody of their daughter.

The family turmoil engulfed Miller’s campaign heading into Election Day and heightened the Democrats’ hopes that they could pick up a red seat.

Like other Democrats around the country, Poindexter also appeared to benefit from the economic volatility and high cost of living that’s accompanied Trump’s second term.

Miller is a former Trump aide, and Poindexter highlighted the connection, hammering home his case that the country’s inflationary trends are the direct result of global tariffs, the Iran war and other specific Trump policies.

The House Republican sought to defuse that message by pointing to the Republicans’ legislative successes under Trump, most notably the sweeping tax cuts signed by the president last year, which included the elimination of taxes on tips and overtime.

It wasn’t enough to save him, however, from restive voters in the 7th District, who sent a clear message Tuesday.

articles.title: Rutinel ousts GOP’s Evans in toss-up Colorado House race
articles.summary: Democrat Manny Rutinel is projected to oust Rep. Gabe Evans (R-Colo.) from his seat in Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Rutinel was leading with 56 percent of the vote with 78 percent of the total reported, according to DDHQ as of 11:18 p.m. EST. Rutinel, a former Colorado state representative,…
articles.body:
Democrat Manny Rutinel is projected to oust Rep. Gabe Evans (R-Colo.) from his seat in Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Rutinel was leading with 56 percent of the vote with 78 percent of the total reported, according to DDHQ as of 11:18 p.m. EST.

Rutinel, a former Colorado state representative , flipped the seat that Evans flipped only two years prior. Rutinel is an attorney and former economist for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.

With Rutinel’s defeat of Evans, who was considered one of the most vulnerable Republicans this election cycle, he has limited the Republican one House term. Cook Political Report rated the Evans-Rutinel match-up as a “toss-up” in mid-October.

During the Democratic primary, Rutinel was mostly aligned with his challenger, former state Rep. Shannon Bird, on most issues, but immigration became a key issue in the race. About 40 percent of the 8th District is Latino.

Rutinel went after Bird for a committee vote she made a year ago against legislation aiming to limit localities from handing over personal identifying information to federal immigration enforcement officials.

President Trump, whose unpopularity has been an issue in this year’s midterms, endorsed Evans back in April 2025, saying in a post on Truth Social that Evans was “an America First Patriot who is doing a fantastic job representing Colorado’s 8th Congressional District!”

“Gabe Evans has my Complete and Total Endorsement for Re-Election — HE WILL NOT LET YOU DOWN!” Trump said at the time.

Shannon Bird, during a debate between Democratic candidates running for Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, May 28, 2026, in Greeley, Colo.

articles.title: Nunn succumbs to Democrat in battleground Iowa House race
articles.summary: Democratic state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott is projected to defeat Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa), according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), flipping Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District back to Democrats after two terms of Republican control. Trone Garriott, a Lutheran minister from West Des Moines, unseated the two-term incumbent in a purple district that includes Des Moines…
articles.body:
Democratic state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott is projected to defeat Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa), according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), flipping Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District back to Democrats after two terms of Republican control.

Trone Garriott, a Lutheran minister from West Des Moines, unseated the two-term incumbent in a purple district that includes Des Moines and the fast-growing suburbs of Dallas County.

DDHQ projected that Trone Garriott beat Nunn by 9 percentage points with 88 percent of the vote counted at 11:22 p.m. EST.

Nunn first flipped the seat for Republicans in 2022, narrowly ousting former Rep. Cindy Axne (D-Iowa) by less than a percentage point. He secured a second term in 2024 against Democrat Lancon Baccam by nearly 4 percentage points in a district President Trump carried by 4.5 points that same year.

Despite Nunn’s previous victories, the district remained one of the most difficult of Iowa’s four congressional seats for Republicans to hold and a major battleground, particularly as Democrats gained momentum heading into the midterm elections.

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report moved the race from “toss-up” to “lean Democrat” in October, citing the difficult political environment facing Nunn despite his strength as an incumbent and Trone Garriott’s polling advantage.

In the final weeks of the campaign, Nunn sought to distance himself from Trump despite receiving his endorsement, voting in favor of a war powers resolution that would limit the president’s military operations against Iran without congressional approval. He also introduced a bill blocking beef imports, breaking with the administration on trade policy.

Trone Garriott, who served in the Iowa state Senate since 2021, outraised Nunn during the campaign. She brought in nearly $8.1 through the final weeks of the midterm election, compared with Nunn’s $6.1 million. Democrats attacked Nunn over his corporate PAC donations, airing advertisements accusing him of receiving financial support from Chinese-owned companies.

Republicans, meanwhile, focused their attacks on Trone Garriott’s record in the Iowa Senate, particularly her vote against legislation banning gender-affirming health care for minors.

Trone Garriott had responded with advertisements of her own pushing back on the criticism, including one in which she said she opposed “letting men in women’s locker rooms.”

The Democrat made healthcare and affordability central issues in her campaign, criticizing Nunn’s support for Republicans’ sweeping tax and spending law and warning that its Medicaid provisions would hurt rural communities in Iowa.

images.caption: Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa) addresses as he leaves the House Chamber following the last votes of the week on June 30, 2026.

articles.title: McGowan wins Iowa House race for open Feenstra seat
articles.summary: Chris McGowan is set to succeed Rep. Randy Feenstra (R) in representing Iowa’s 4th Congressional District, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) has projected. McGowan led Democratic opponent Dave Dawson by almost 26 percentage points — 62.9 to 37.1 percent — with 68 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 11:22 p.m. EST on Tuesday.…
articles.body:
Chris McGowan is set to succeed Rep. Randy Feenstra (R) in representing Iowa’s 4th Congressional District, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) has projected.

McGowan led Democratic opponent Dave Dawson by almost 26 percentage points — 62.9 to 37.1 percent — with 68 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 11:22 p.m. EST on Tuesday.

McGowan, an Air Force veteran, has a history in consulting GOP candidates on multiple levels, including in the federal, state and local races. He makes a return to Capitol Hill after previously being a congressional intern when he was a college student back in 1987.

Feenstra, who has served in Congress since 2021, ran in the Iowa governor’s race this year but lost in the primary to Republican business owner Zach Lahn.

President Trump endorsed McGowan earlier this year in his bid for Congress, calling him a “fantastic Candidate.”

“A Brave Iowa Air National Guard Veteran, successful Attorney, and now, as President of the Siouxland Chamber of Commerce, Chris has a Proven Record of Success — He is a WINNER!” Trump wrote on Truth Social in February.

“Chris McGowan has my Complete and Total Endorsement to be the next Representative from Iowa’s 4th Congressional District, HE WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” he added later.

McGowan’s path to victory Tuesday appeared easy, with the nonpartisan political handicapper Cook Political Report rating his race as solidly Republican.

articles.title: Miller-Meeks loses reelection in battleground Iowa House race
articles.summary: Democrat Christina Bohannan is projected to unseat Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R) in the race for Iowa’s 1st Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ, flipping a key battleground seat for Democrats. Bohannan, a University of Iowa law professor and former state lawmaker, defeated the three-term Republican in their third consecutive general election match-up after narrowly…
articles.body:
Democrat Christina Bohannan is projected to unseat Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R) in the race for Iowa’s 1st Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ, flipping a key battleground seat for Democrats.

Bohannan, a University of Iowa law professor and former state lawmaker, defeated the three-term Republican in their third consecutive general election match-up after narrowly losing to Miller-Meeks in 2022 and 2024.

The victory comes two years after Miller-Meeks defeated Bohannan by just 799 votes in 2024, one of the closest House races in history. The results were confirmed after a recount, allowing Miller-Meeks to secure another term in Congress.

Miller-Meeks also won her 2020 election bid to Congress by just six votes, defeating Democrat Rita Hart in what was then Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District.

The southeastern Iowa district, which includes Iowa City, Davenport and Burlington, emerged as one of the most competitive House races in recent election cycles. President Trump, who endorsed Miller-Meeks, carried the district by more than 8 percentage points in 2024.

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report moved the race from “toss up” to “lean Democrat” in October, citing Miller-Meeks’s unpopularity and growing challenges in the political environment for Republicans as she sought a fourth term.

Both parties poured millions of dollars into the race. The Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with House Republican leadership, spent $5 million on television and digital advertising. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) joined Miller-Meeks on the campaign trail and has described the district as one of the most consequential battlegrounds.

Bohannan, meanwhile, emerged as a fundraising juggernaut, spending nearly $5 million on television advertising while the Democratic-aligned House Majority PAC planned another $4 million in spending.

Democrats targeted Miller-Meeks over her support for the Trump administration’s tariffs, arguing that the policies had hurt Iowa’s agriculture-heavy economy. Bohannan, who previously served in the Iowa state House, campaigned on lowering costs for working families and protecting access to healthcare. She also criticized Miller-Meeks for supporting sweeping tax and spending legislation.

Bohannan’s victory ends Miller-Meeks’s tenure in Congress and delivers Democrats a closely watched pickup in their effort to win back the House majority.

articles.title: LA County Supervisor Hilda Solis wins open California House seat
articles.summary: Los Angeles County Supervisor Hilda Solis (D) is projected to win the seat to lead California’s 38th Congressional District, drawn up after Golden State voters passed the state’s redistricting ballot measure last year, according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Solis defeated Republican Pedro Casas as the two sought to lead a district…
articles.body:
Los Angeles County Supervisor Hilda Solis (D) is projected to win the seat to lead California’s 38th Congressional District, drawn up after Golden State voters passed the state’s redistricting ballot measure last year, according to preliminary results from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Solis defeated Republican Pedro Casas as the two sought to lead a district formerly led by Rep. Linda Sanchez (D), who filed to run in California’s 41st Congressional District after voters approved Proposition 50 last November. The two ran in a district that the Cook Political Report said was solidly in favor of Democrats.

With nearly 60 percent of ballots counted, Solis had captured 66 percent of the vote, DDHQ reported .

The 38th District straddles Los Angeles and Orange counties, encompassing cities like Diamond Bar, Industry, Pico Rivera, Montebello and Whittier, which includes the family home of former President Nixon.

A native Angeleno, Solis campaigned on defending communities she said were “under assault by the Trump administration –– and I won’t just stand by and let it happen.” She ran on defending women’s reproductive rights, organized labor, immigrant rights and access to healthcare.

“I wish Proposition 50 wasn’t necessary – but Trump and his allies in Texas and elsewhere are undermining our democracy,” she said on her campaign website , referring to California’s state measure redrawing its congressional map approved by voters last year. “We must fight fire with fire, because too much is at stake.”

Solis secured several endorsements from Democratic leaders across the state, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, Los Angeles County Sheriff Robert Luna, and Chicano rights icon and leader Dolores Huerta.

Solis previously served as former President Obama’s Labor secretary during his first term. Before that, she served in the House from 2001 to 2009, representing California’s 31st and 33rd districts. She became the first Hispanic woman elected to the California state Senate in 1994.

articles.title: Lindsay James wins in Iowa, turning Hinson’s House seat blue
articles.summary: Iowa state Rep. Lindsay James (D) is projected to defeat Republican Joe Mitchell in the state’s 2nd Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). James’s victory turns a Republican-held seat blue after Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) opted to run for Senate, giving Democrats a pickup in their fight for control of the House. The…
articles.body:
Iowa state Rep. Lindsay James (D) is projected to defeat Republican Joe Mitchell in the state’s 2nd Congressional District , according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

James’s victory turns a Republican-held seat blue after Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) opted to run for Senate, giving Democrats a pickup in their fight for control of the House.

The result comes as voters grew frustrated over rising gas prices tied to the ongoing Iran war and President Trump’s handling of the economy .

DDHQ’s preelection forecast rated the race a toss-up, giving Mitchell a 53 percent chance of winning compared to James’s 47 percent.

James, a Presbyterian pastor from Dubuque, campaigned heavily on affordability, arguing that Trump’s tariffs and the GOP’s sweeping tax and spending law were squeezing families in the Hawkeye State.

Mitchell, a former Iowa state lawmaker and Trump administration housing official, pitched lower taxes and his experience as a housing developer as solutions to rising costs.

The Democrat’s victory marks a notable shift in a state that has moved sharply toward Republicans over the past decade, giving her party a foothold in northeastern Iowa.

Her win comes in a district the president, who backed her rival, carried by roughly 10 percentage points in 2024.

Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) has conceded to Democrat Cait Conley in the race to represent New York’s 17th Congressional District, as a key battleground seat is now poised to flip and add to Democrats newly projected House advantage. The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ has not yet called the race. “When all of the votes…
articles.body:
Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) has conceded to Democrat Cait Conley in the race to represent New York’s 17th Congressional District, as a key battleground seat is now poised to flip and add to Democrats newly projected House advantage .

The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ has not yet called the race.

“When all of the votes are counted tomorrow in Westchester it’s going to be pretty clear we’re going to be short,” Lawler told supporters on Tuesday night. “I have never been afforded in any of my elections a concession on election night and I fundamentally believe it’s the right thing to do. And so I congratulate Cait on her win and wish her well as our next member of Congress.”

The race drew national attention and significant financial resources from both parties, as Republicans sought to preserve their narrow majority in the lower chamber.

Lawler sought to cast himself as a bipartisan lawmaker willing to work across the aisle, while Conley distanced herself from the left flank of her party and sought to capitalize on voter dissatisfaction with President Trump and his administration, particularly over the economy and the war in Iran.

Lawler’s defeat marks a major setback for House Republicans as Democrats notch a key pickup.

During his time in Congress, Lawler occasionally broke from his party on high-profile issues and sought to position himself as a moderate voice in a deeply divided House.

He was among four Republicans who signed a Democratic-backed discharge petition to force a vote on legislation that would extend the now-expired Affordable Care Act subsidies for three years. He also championed efforts to lift the cap on state and local tax deductions, a particularly significant issue for his district.

Lawler also clashed with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) during a heated showdown last year amid the government shutdown. Their exchange went viral on social media, underscoring the tensions between the two New York lawmakers.

In perhaps one of the more unusual endorsements of the race, Lawler secured the backing of Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine). But those cross-party credentials ultimately were not enough to save his seat.

Conley, meanwhile, secured endorsements from several national organizations and PACs, including the League of Conservation Voters, the Planned Parenthood Action Fund and Defend the Vote. Jeffries had also stumped for her on the campaign trail.

She sought to distance herself from the Democratic Socialists of America, of which New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) is a member. During a September debate, Conley said she had “firm disagreements” with members of the organization.

images.caption: Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) heads to the Capitol for the last series of votes before the August recess on July 23, 2026.

articles.title: Gray wins open Wyoming House seat
articles.summary: Wyoming Secretary of State Chuck Gray (R) is projected to win the race to represent the state’s at-large congressional district, according to Decision Desk HQ. The state election official defeated Democrat Lisa Kinney, the former state Senate minority leader, in a seat considered safe for Republicans. He will succeed Republican Rep. Harriet Hageman, who is…
articles.body:
Wyoming Secretary of State Chuck Gray (R) is projected to win the race to represent the state’s at-large congressional district, according to Decision Desk HQ .

The state election official defeated Democrat Lisa Kinney, the former state Senate minority leader, in a seat considered safe for Republicans. He will succeed Republican Rep. Harriet Hageman, who is running for Senate.

Gray led Kinney by more than 31 percentage points — 59 to nearly 28 percent — with 37 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 11:40 p.m. Tuesday.

Gray was elected as Wyoming’s secretary of state in 2022. He previously represented District 57 in the state House from 2017 to 2023.

The Republican secretary of state is known for his staunch support of conservative values. His campaign website highlights efforts to enact anti-abortion legislation at the state level, as well as advocacy to protect fossil fuel industry jobs.

Voter ID legislation and restrictions have also been a top priority for Gray as secretary of state. However, some of his proposals were rejected by Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon (R), who said the measures exceeded the legal authority granted to his office.

Gray has supported President Trump’s false claim that widespread fraud occurred in the 2020 election. In 2021, he made a trip to Arizona to view a partisan audit of the presidential election.

Gray previously ran in the Republican primary in 2022 to oust former Rep. Liz Cheney (R). He dropped out of the race after Trump backed Hageman.

images.caption: Chuck Gray, Wyoming secretary of state, testifies during a House Committee on House Administration hearing on federal elections on Capitol Hill, Feb. 10, 2026, in Washington.

articles.title: Ohio approves photo ID requirement to vote
articles.summary: A ballot measure that would enshrine photo identification requirements to vote in the Ohio Constitution is projected to pass, according to Decision Desk HQ. The constitutional amendment, known as Issue 3, will require voters to show government-issued photo ID in order to cast a ballot. With 87 percent of ballots counted, 66 percent of voters…
articles.body:
A ballot measure that would enshrine photo identification requirements to vote in the Ohio Constitution is projected to pass, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The constitutional amendment, known as Issue 3, will require voters to show government-issued photo ID in order to cast a ballot.

With 87 percent of ballots counted, 66 percent of voters approved of Issue 3, DDHQ reported .

Acceptable forms of government-issued photo ID include: “an unexpired Ohio driver license or state identification card; a United States passport or passport card; or a United States military identification card, Ohio National Guard identification card, or United States Department of Veterans Affairs identification card.”

The initiative will also require those casting mail-in or absentee ballots to show a form of government-issued photo ID “unless the law authorizes those persons to vote by providing a signature and at least one other specified unique identifier.”

The constitutional amendment will allow voters to seek a religious exception if they have a “religious objection” to being photographed and don’t have government-issued photo ID, allowing the state to provide “an alternative method” for verifying the voter’s identity.

Ohio law already requires voters to show photo ID to cast a ballot ; the ballot measure enshrines those requirements in the state constitution.

Ohio law also allows for religious exemptions around issuing photo ID at the polls, instead requiring voters to sign an affidavit swearing that they don’t have a form of photo ID for religious reasons, and they must provide the last four numbers of their Social Security number.

Ballotpedia notes that more than a dozen states are teeing up ballot measures pertaining to election policy, including six states that are asking voters about voting and citizenship and six states asking about voter ID.

articles.title: Tedford wins Oklahoma election to replace House’s Hern

Tedford beat his Democratic opponent, John Croisant, for the seat Hern left open after he decided to run for Oklahoma’s open Senate seat, which was previously occupied by…
articles.body:
Oklahoma state Rep. Mark Tedford (R) is projected to win the state’s 1st Congressional District election to replace Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Okla.), according to Decision Desk HQ .

Tedford beat his Democratic opponent, John Croisant, for the seat Hern left open after he decided to run for Oklahoma’s open Senate seat, which was previously occupied by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

The Republican led Croisant by just under five percentage points — 52.3 to 47.7 percent — with 90 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 11:47 p.m. Tuesday.

Tedford has positioned himself as the establishment conservative choice. He was also endorsed by the Oklahoma House Speaker and the three Tulsa County commissioners.

He campaigned on strict enforcement of immigration laws, reducing inflationary spending, eliminating waste and fraud on the federal level and provisions focused on rebuilding the American economy, according to his campaign website .

The House seat has been held by Republicans since 1987 and was carried by President Trump in each of his presidential bids. The president did not endorse Tedford at first, instead choosing to back Jackson Lahmeyer, a Tulsa pastor.

Lahmeyer enjoyed a close relationship with the Trump family, even hosting some family members at his church. He dropped out of the primaries after the Daily Mail published intimate text messages between Lahmeyer and a woman who was not his wife, in which he called her “cute” and invited her to his hotel room.

While Lahmeyer argued on Facebook the messages were “carefully cherry-picked to create an impression that is not accurate,” he dropped out of the primaries as Trump rescinded his endorsement, choosing to back Tedford.

“I greatly appreciate Jackson Lahmeyer’s hard work under difficult circumstances — He has always been with me, and I will always be with him,” the president wrote on Truth Social. “But, when it comes to the current Congressional race for Oklahoma’s 1st Congressional District, I will be supporting America First Patriot, Mark Tedford.”

articles.body:
A ballot measure that would ​specify that only U.S. citizens are allowed to vote in Kansas, making a mild language change to the state’s existing citizenship voting requirement, is projected to pass, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Voters approved the constitutional amendment, which tweaks language in the Kansas Constitution from saying “Every citizen of the United States” who has reached 18 years old and resides in the area they’re looking to vote in are qualified electors to instead saying “No person shall be deemed a qualified elector unless such person” is a U.S. citizen, has reached 18 years old and resides in the area they’re looking to vote in.

DDHQ projected that the measure passed by almost 25 percentage points with 90 percent of votes counted at 11:50 p.m. EST.

Kansas law already states it is a crime for someone who is not a U.S. citizen to vote in an election, but the ballot measure looks to make that requirement even clearer.

Noncitizens are not allowed to vote in federal elections, and only a small group of municipalities, in addition to Washington, D.C., allow them to vote in certain elections, according to Ballotpedia .

Republicans have leaned into issues around voting and proper identification , particularly as President Trump has baselessly asserted there’s been widespread voter fraud .

The president has pressed GOP lawmakers to pass legislation that would require people show proof of citizenship to register to vote and show photo identification at the polls, though those efforts have been unsuccessful.

Ballotpedia also notes that more than a dozen states are teeing up ballot measures pertaining to election policy, including six states asking voters about voting and citizenship and another six states asking about voter ID.

articles.title: Democrats, long in the dumps, revel in midterm rout over GOP
articles.summary: Jubilant House Democrats celebrated their midterm rout on Tuesday night in Washington, reveling in the voters’ resounding rejection of the reigning Republicans and vowing to escalate their battles with President Trump just as soon as they take power in the earliest days of next year. Gathered at the AC Hotel, a trendy Marriott property in…
articles.body:
Jubilant House Democrats celebrated their midterm rout on Tuesday night in Washington, reveling in the voters’ resounding rejection of the reigning Republicans and vowing to escalate their battles with President Trump just as soon as they take power in the earliest days of next year.

Gathered at the AC Hotel, a trendy Marriott property in the trendy Navy Yard section of Washington, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and other Democratic leaders portrayed the outcome as a repudiation of Trump’s turbulent return to office. And they greeted the results with a level of exuberance that’s been dormant over the past two years as they’ve roamed without much power in the minority wilderness.

“Today begins the great American comeback,” Jeffries told the cheering crowd. “This is a change election, and we understand as House Democrats that we need to deliver dramatic change.”

The Democrats’ watch party, just a few blocks from the U.S. Capitol, was more subdued than those of cycle’s past — at least initially.

Throughout the day, Democratic operatives worked the phones in a final push to nudge battleground voters to the polls. Only after 8 p.m. did a few dozen young staffers turn their attention to the news networks broadcasting the returns. The bar was open, but almost no one was drinking.

That changed as the results began to trickle in, showing the momentum clearly shifting in the Democrats’ favor.

Incumbents clung to seats in Florida and Ohio that were redistricted to knock them off. Challengers flipped GOP seats in Kentucky and North Carolina that Trump had carried by double digits. And inside the AC Hotel, the Democrats’ anxious hopes shifted to open revelry on the news that restive voters were on track to put them in control of both chambers in the next Congress.

Then, shortly after 9:30 p.m., CNN broadcast live from the event, and the room exploded. That was followed, at 10:05 p.m., by CNN’s announcement that Democrats had seized House control. The chants began immediately: “Jeffries! Jeffries! Jeffries!”

The Democrats’ victory was not a surprise.

Heading into Tuesday, polls, pundits and election handicappers predicted that Democrats would not only win, but win big. And Jeffries and other party leaders were publicly bullish that the House was theirs to lose.

Still, polls, pundits and election handicappers have been wrong before, and Democrats have burned themselves more than once over the last decade by undercounting Trump’s supporters and overestimating their own.

Those disappointing showings have been at the front of Democrats’ minds this year, and many of them have been treading cautiously into Tuesday, careful not to overpromise or take anything for granted. After voting in New York, Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer (D-N.Y.) summed up the sentiments of his party: “We are nauseously optimistic,” he said.

The exuberant mood late Tuesday marked a dramatic shift for a party that’s had little to celebrate through the first half of Trump’s second term, when the majority Republicans powered through a host of their legislative priorities — most notably, last year’s massive package of tax cuts, Medicaid cuts and immigration enforcement funding — and Trump has operated virtually unchecked by the GOP-led Congress.

Many of those policies, however, appeared to backfire on the GOP on Tuesday. The Iran War has splintered Trump’s MAGA coalition. His deportation surge has eliminated the gains he’d made with Hispanic voters in 2024. His efforts to scale back race-based voting protections might have animated Black voters in key districts. His tariffs have alienated traditional free-market conservatives. And the increase in consumer costs during his term has angered many working-class populists who supported him in the past, including farmers who’ve been clobbered by Trump’s trade wars and the spike in diesel fuel costs.

Trump, who was watching the returns from the White House, had hand-picked some of the GOP candidates who lost, particularly those in the Senate. The White House blamed the candidates for running lackluster campaigns.

The midterm wave marked a major victory for Jeffries, who rose to the top Democratic leadership spot four years ago but has come under fire this cycle from liberals who think he’s done too little to push back against Trump. He’s also had big shoes to fill, following the long reign of Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), a liberal icon and the first female Speaker in U.S. history.

But Jeffries was disciplined throughout the cycle, keeping his diverse caucus largely united in opposition to Trump’s policy agenda, while fighting to ensure the focus of the campaign remained centered around the issue of affordability — a topic of universal interest that seemed to help Democrats up and down the ballot.

The Democrats’ victory puts him in line to become the first Black Speaker in U.S. history, a vote that will take place on Jan. 3. In that role, Jeffries will face his own challenges managing an ideologically diverse caucus. Tuesday’s results, however, will give him a comfortable cushion with which to operate, eroding the leverage of the democratic socialists and other small blocs of lawmakers who might band together with designs to demand their priorities.
