articles.title: Maryland approves amendment making it easier to redistrict House map
articles.summary: A ballot measure that would make it easier for Maryland Democrats to pass a more favorable House map is projected to pass, according to Decision Desk HQ. Voters approved the constitutional amendment, known as Question 3, which would enact different requirements for drawing maps for state legislative seats and congressional districts. The initiative will also…
articles.body:
A ballot measure that would make it easier for Maryland Democrats to pass a more favorable House map is projected to pass, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Voters approved the constitutional amendment, known as Question 3, which would enact different requirements for drawing maps for state legislative seats and congressional districts. The initiative will also require state legislative districts to be compact and adjoining, but there would be no criteria for determining how to draw the lines.

It is projected to pass with 59.65 percent support, while 40.35 percent opposed, with 94 percent reported by DDHQ.

The ballot measure also gives the General Assembly “the power to grant original jurisdiction to the Supreme Court of Maryland to review the congressional districting plan of the state.”

The Old Line State has a Democratic-favored 7-1 congressional delegation, with Rep. Andy Harris (Md.) as the state’s lone Republican. Democrats tried to redistrict the state’s congressional map earlier this year in response to GOP-led redistricting in states like Texas and Missouri as Republicans looked to add pickup opportunities for themselves in the upper chamber of Congress.

A new map would have only offered Maryland Democrats at least one pickup opportunity.

Maryland Senate President Bill Ferguson (D) blocked his party’s efforts to redraw a new House map ahead of the 2026 elections, worrying that Democrats could see a repeat scenario of 2022 — when the party tried to aggressively usher in an 8-0 gerrymander that later got struck down by the courts.

Ferguson, however, appeared to shift his stance in May, suggesting he would be open to moving forward with a constitutional amendment to tee up before voters as the Senate president braced for a competitive primary that he ultimately won in June.

articles.body:
Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) is projected to win the state’s Senate race, defeating Republican challenger Michele Tafoya, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Flanagan, who has served as the state’s lieutenant governor since 2019, will replace retiring Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minn.). Flanagan is projected to win with nearly 55 percent support, with just under 70 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ.

She faced an uphill battle in this race as her Republican opponent sought to blame her for a widespread fraud scandal that played out during her time working under Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D).

The Democrat responded to these accusations during an October debate, agreeing with Walz’s assessment that “more should have been done sooner” to halt the scheme, in which prosecutors say as much as $9 billion was stolen.

Walz dropped his reelection bid for the state’s top executive office amid scrutiny over his handling of this fraud scandal.

However, the criticism did not prove enough to turn the state’s open Senate seat red, with the Democrat maintaining a narrow lead in polling leading up to Election Day.

Flanagan campaigned in support of issues like “Medicare for All,” universal childcare, raising the minimum wage and expanding healthcare for veterans.

Additionally, the Minnesota Democrat pushed back on President Trump’s tariffs against Canada and called to “dismantle” U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and end the Trump administration’s mass deportation policy.

articles.summary: Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) was projected to defeat state House Speaker Lisa Demuth (R) in Minnesota’s governor’s race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), becoming the first woman elected to lead the state. The four-term Democratic senator will succeed outgoing Gov. Tim Walz (D), who dropped his bid for a third term in January as…
articles.body:
Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) was projected to defeat state House Speaker Lisa Demuth (R) in Minnesota’s governor’s race , according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), becoming the first woman elected to lead the state.

The four-term Democratic senator will succeed outgoing Gov. Tim Walz (D), who dropped his bid for a third term in January as fraud scandals involving state social service programs plagued his administration and fueled attacks from President Trump and other Republicans.

The Democrat notched just over 56 percent of the vote, with under 70 percent of the vote tallied early Wednesday by DDHQ.

The controversies became a significant issue on the campaign trail, with both candidates promising greater oversight.

Klobuchar touted her background as a prosecutor and said she would order a full audit of the state government, while Demuth pledged to clean house and replace all state agency commissioners. The GOP candidate also sought to cast blame on Democratic leaders, accusing them of allowing a culture of fraud and waste to fester.

The candidates also clashed over the Trump administration’s crackdown on immigration in the North Star State, where federal officers shot and killed two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti. Klobuchar condemned the killings and called for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to leave the state.

Demuth called the deaths tragic and urged full investigations but defended the broader ICE operation.

Klobuchar entered the final days of the race as the clear favorite. The Democrat has represented Minnesota in the U.S. Senate since 2007, winning all four of her elections by double digits.

Cook Political Report had rated the race as “solid Democrat,” and DDHQ gave Klobuchar a 91 percent chance of winning the race heading into Election Day.

She easily won the Democratic nomination, while Demuth clinched the GOP nod after defeating Trump-backed MyPillow founder Mike Lindell, a prominent proponent of false claims that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. Lindell also unsuccessfully asked for a recount after the loss in August.

articles.title: McGuire flips California House seat in redistricting shake-up
articles.summary: Democrat Mike McGuire is projected to win California’s 1st District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). McGuire defeated Republican Rep. James Gallagher, flipping a Northern California seat that became a prime Democratic pickup opportunity following a contentious redistricting battle. For Gallagher, the defeat marks an abrupt end to a short stint in Washington. DDHQ reported…
articles.body:
Democrat Mike McGuire is projected to win California’s 1st District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

McGuire defeated Republican Rep. James Gallagher, flipping a Northern California seat that became a prime Democratic pickup opportunity following a contentious redistricting battle . For Gallagher, the defeat marks an abrupt end to a short stint in Washington.

DDHQ reported McGuire leading Gallagher by over 16 points with 49 percent of ballots counted.

The Republican won a special election in June to replace Rep. Doug LaMalfa (R-Calif.), who died in January after representing the region for more than a decade.

But the district Gallagher won over the summer looked dramatically different from the one voters weighed in on this week.

California voters approved Proposition 50 late last year, temporarily redrawing the state’s congressional map in response to a Republican-led redistricting push that began in Texas at President Trump’s urging.

The new boundaries brought more Democratic voters into the 1st District, including portions of Sonoma and Mendocino counties, while shifting several Republican strongholds into neighboring districts.

Under the previous boundaries, Trump carried the district by roughly 25 percentage points in 2024. The new map would have favored former Vice President Kamala Harris by approximately 12 points.

DDHQ rated the race as “safe Democratic” ahead of Election Day.

McGuire, a California state Senate leader, has served in the state Legislature since 2014 and previously held local offices in Sonoma County, including mayor of Healdsburg, Calif. His campaign focused heavily on opposition to Trump’s agenda, including federal healthcare cuts and tariffs, while also emphasizing wildfire prevention and affordability.

Gallagher, meanwhile, criticized the redistricting effort and sought to highlight his record representing rural Northern California communities.

articles.body:
Democratic Rep. Don Davis (N.C.) is projected to hold on to his House seat after it was redrawn to favor Republicans in a GOP-led redistricting effort in North Carolina, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The Tar Heel State’s 1st District was redrawn last year to include communities that have historically supported Republican candidates. Davis is projected to defeat Republican challenger Laurie Buckhout to hold the seat.

Davis led Buckhout by 2 percentage points — 49 to 47 percent — with 93 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 12:16 a.m. Tuesday.

Davis, who is an Air Force veteran and a Presbyterian lay minister, previously bested Buckhout in 2024 prior to the state’s redistricting effort.

During his time in the House, the two-term lawmaker has carved out a reputation as a centrist Democrat. He was among the 14 members of his party to back this year’s GOP-authored farm bill, and he has also supported bipartisan legislation to expand resources for veterans and to strengthen the U.S.’s relationship with Israel.

The Democrat campaigned on lowering prescription drug costs, expanding affordable housing, investing in rural infrastructure, increasing education access and improving veteran services.

articles.summary: President Trump congratulated Democrats on their midterm election wins Tuesday night. articles.body:
President Trump congratulated Democrats on their midterm election wins Tuesday night.

Trump, in a call with CBS News , said that his message is “congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country.”

He told the outlet that he “wasn’t on the ballot, and there was nothing that could be done about that.”

Democrats won control of the House and Senate Tuesday night, grabbing hold of some key races like the Texas, South Carolina and Kansas Senate seats, among others.

Trump told Fox News that voters just “didn’t like the candidates.”

“They fought hard. They’ve been fighting for a long time,” he said.

He also said he could work with Democrats on “many things.”

Still, he said he felt bad for the Republicans that lost Tuesday night because losing is a “tough thing.”

Earlier Tuesday, Trump said Republicans lost because he wasn’t on the ballot.

“And if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” he wrote on Truth Social. “Thank you for your attention to this matter.”

In another post he said he would become a “Political Pundit, both good and bad, on the reasons these Candidates won and lost!”

One Democrat — incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) — shared a succinct statement after it was clear Democrats were winning: “Lawyer up.”

DDHQ called the vote at 12:15 a.m. EST Wednesday, with 62 percent of votes counted. The ballot breakdown was…
articles.body:
A ballot measure that would stipulate only U.S. citizens can register and vote in Arizona elections and ban foreign nationals from contributing to elections in the state is projected to fail, according to Decision Desk HQ.

DDHQ called the vote at 12:15 a.m. EST Wednesday, with 62 percent of votes counted. The ballot breakdown was around 56 percent in favor of the proposition, 44 percent opposed.

Voters rejected the constitutional amendment, known as Proposition 144 , which would mandate that only U.S. citizens can register and vote in the elections in the Grand Canyon State, ban foreign contributions in Arizona elections, require government-issued proof of identification to cast in-person and mail-in ballots and allow voters to have their ballots tabulated at their polling location on the day of the election.

Arizona passed a measure in 2004 that required proof of citizenship in order to register to vote, though the Supreme Court ruled in 2013 that the National Voter Registration Act invalidated that requirement for voters using the federal form to register.

The state’s law currently requires either a form of photo ID or two forms of certain identification documents without a photo in order to cast a ballot early or on Election Day.

Noncitizens are not allowed to vote in federal elections, and only a small group of municipalities in addition to Washington, D.C., allow them to vote in certain elections, according to Ballotpedia .

Republicans have leaned into issues around voting and proper identification , particularly as President Trump has asserted without basis that there has been widespread voter fraud .

The president has pressed GOP lawmakers to pass legislation that would require people to show proof of citizenship in order to register to vote and show photo identification at the polls, though those efforts have been unsuccessful.

Ballotpedia notes that 15 states are teeing up ballot measures next week pertaining to election policy, including six states that are asking voters about voting and citizenship and six states asking about voter ID.

The nation’s highest court is expected to hear a case this fall around whether Arizona can mandate proof of citizenship as a requirement for voter registration.

articles.title: Virginia repeals same-sex marriage ban from state constitution
articles.summary: Virginia voters have approved a measure repealing language from the state constitution restricting same-sex marriage, Decision Desk HQ projects. The amendment removes a provision stating that marriage is only between a man and a woman and prohibits the state from denying a marriage license to two adults because of their sex, gender or race. A…
articles.body:
Virginia voters have approved a measure repealing language from the state constitution restricting same-sex marriage , Decision Desk HQ projects.

The amendment removes a provision stating that marriage is only between a man and a woman and prohibits the state from denying a marriage license to two adults because of their sex, gender or race.

A federal judge struck down the ban as unconstitutional in 2014, and same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the Supreme Court’s 2015 ruling in Obergefell v. Hodges. The high court also rejected an appeal of the decision last year.

Now, the successful measure formally takes the restriction off the books in Virginia.

Some advocates have expressed concern that Obergefell could be overturned following the court’s 2022 decision overturning Roe v. Wade.

In a concurring opinion, Justice Clarence Thomas suggested the court should review other cases decided with similar legal reasoning, including the 2015 case. Other justices, however, did not join that opinion.

A few other states have also repealed their bans on same-sex marriage in recent years. Nevada was the first to do so in 2020, and California, Colorado and Hawaii followed suit in 2024.

articles.body:
Former podcaster Fred Wellman (D) is projected to defeat incumbent Rep. Ann Wagner (R-Mo.) in a congressional district President Trump carried by nearly 8 points in 2024, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), The Hill’s election partner.

Wellman leads Wagner by about 7 points, with more than 95 percent of precincts reporting, per DDHQ.

Wagner has represented Missouri’s 2nd Congressional District for seven terms but faced trouble in an election cycle that put dozens of House Republicans on the defensive.

Wellman is an Army veteran and stated previously that recent legislative decisions have pushed him to enter the congressional race. Wellman also hosts “ On Democracy ” which is a MeidasTouch network podcast.

“When I decided to run for Congress it was driven by one thing: seeing so many people in my family and community struggling to survive while our representatives looked down at us as less than them,” he wrote on social media Tuesday.

The Democrat wrote that his three goals in Congress were to lower costs, fight corruption and end “the chaos in DC”

“We deserve better. Choose hope over division today,” he concluded.

His other campaign promises included lowering Medicare eligibility while also expanding coverage of the program.

Notably, Wagner outspent Wellman $5.7 million to $2.2 million, according to a Fox affiliate station , citing Federal Election Commission filings.

The win marks the first time Democrats have won the seat since 1990.

articles.body:
Virginia voters passed a “reproductive freedom” ballot measure Tuesday, enshrining current protections — including abortion — into the state constitution, Decision Desk HQ projects.

The amendment puts protections for abortion, birth control, and in-vitro fertilization into the state constitution. It also protects fertility care, pregnancy-related care, and miscarriage care.

The amendment makes abortion legal up to the third trimester, at which point the procedure is only allowed if the fetus is not viable or a physician considers an abortion necessary to protect the health of the fetus or mother.

Virginia is the only state in the south not to ban abortion at or before 12 weeks of pregnancy.

A Democrat has not won a Senate race since 1974. Risch was the favorite to win Tuesday.

articles.summary: GOP Rep. Julia Letlow is projected to narrowly win her Louisiana Senate race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). She notched about 50 percent of the…
articles.body:
GOP Rep. Julia Letlow is projected to narrowly win her Louisiana Senate race, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

She will be the first Republican woman to represent the Pelican State after she defeated Democratic nominee Jamie Davis in the contest to replace outgoing Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.).

She notched about 50 percent of the vote with 100 percent of the vote reported as of early Wednesday morning. Davis lost by just under 2 percentage points in the solid red state.

Letlow was widely expected to win the seat since emerging from the June primary runoff. In the first round of the primary, she and another challenger backed by President Trump — state Treasurer John Fleming — defeated Cassidy in the GOP primary.

The then-incumbent had battled with Trump over his vote to convict the former president in 2021 and later for the senator’s critical view of the president’s nominees for top administration posts, especially Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as Health and Human Services secretary.

The Democrat, a farmer and former police juror, polled behind the GOP nominee for most of the race.

Letlow, 45, was a higher education administrator when her husband Luke was elected to the state’s 5th Congressional District in 2020. He died from complications of COVID-19 just weeks before he was set to take office.

She then ran and won in the special election for his seat in April 2021. She was reelected twice and announced she would run for Senate in January 2026.

In the House, she has pushed for education-related measures including the Parents Bill of Rights to give parents more consent over public school curricula, which passed the House in 2023. She has also served on the Appropriations Committee.

DDHQ rated the race as likely Republican ahead of Election Day.

articles.summary: A ballot measure that would only allow U.S. citizens who meet certain criteria to vote in elections in Arkansas is projected to pass, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). The “yes” option had about 69 percent of the vote as of 12:30 a.m. EST on Wednesday, per DDHQ. Arkansas voters approved the constitutional amendment, known…
articles.body:
A ballot measure that would only allow U.S. citizens who meet certain criteria to vote in elections in Arkansas is projected to pass, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

The “yes” option had about 69 percent of the vote as of 12:30 a.m. EST on Wednesday, per DDHQ .

Arkansas voters approved the constitutional amendment , known as Issue 1, which says that only U.S. citizens who show a form of photo ID and are at least 18 years old, an Arkansas resident and registered to vote are allowed to vote in elections in the state.

The initiative would add language to the state constitution saying, “A person who does not meet the qualifications of an elector under this section shall not be permitted to vote in any state or local election held in this state.”

The Natural State already requires people to be citizens who meet certain criteria and provide photo ID in order to vote, though the ballot language reinforces these rules by getting rid of language saying that a person who meets the criteria “may” vote, updating it to “only” those who meet the requirements. It also specifies that voters who fall short cannot cast a ballot in either statewide or local elections.

Noncitizens are not allowed to vote in federal elections, and only a small group of municipalities in addition to Washington, D.C., allow them to vote in certain elections, according to Ballotpedia .

Republicans have leaned into issues around voting and proper identification , particularly as President Trump has asserted without basis that there has been widespread voter fraud .

The president has pressed GOP lawmakers to pass legislation that would require people to show proof of citizenship in order to register to vote and show photo identification at the polls, though those efforts have been unsuccessful.

Ballotpedia also notes that more than a dozen states are teeing up ballot measures pertaining to election policy, including six states asking voters about voting and citizenship and another six states asking about voter ID.

articles.title: North Carolina voters approve constitutional amendment requiring photo ID for mail-in ballots
articles.summary: North Carolinians are projected to approve a constitutional amendment requiring that all voters in the state show photo ID to cast a ballot, according to Decision Desk HQ. The Require Photo Identification Amendment proposed changing the North Carolina Constitution to require all voters in the state to present an ID, regardless of whether they are…
articles.body:
North Carolinians are projected to approve a constitutional amendment requiring that all voters in the state show photo ID to cast a ballot, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The Require Photo Identification Amendment proposed changing the North Carolina Constitution to require all voters in the state to present an ID, regardless of whether they are casting a ballot in person or not.

The amendment’s passage represents a win for state Republicans, who backed uniform rules for in-person voters and those who cast their ballot by mail.

It also marks a loss for the state Democratic Party, which cited concerns about the effects of a mail-in photo ID requirement on military members, students, rural residents and the elderly in advocating against the amendment.

North Carolina voters already have to show identification when they cast a ballot in person or by mail. The amendment’s passage, however, enshrines the requirement in the state constitution, making it more difficult for future state lawmakers to overturn it.

Republicans in the North Carolina General Assembly approved the amendment’s addition to this year’s ballot in December 2024. Voters in North Carolina previously amended the state constitution in 2018 to require in-person voters to show photo ID at the polls.

articles.body:
Johnny Garcia (D) is projected to win the race to represent Texas’s 35th Congressional District, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

The district, which was redrawn in the GOP’s favor during a mid-decade redistricting effort led by state Republicans, is represented by Rep. Greg Casar (D). It includes the suburbs of San Antonio and surrounding communities and has a majority-Hispanic population, as well as a large military community.

Garcia, the deputy sheriff in Bexar County, defeated Republican nominee Carlos De La Cruz, an Air Force veteran and brother of Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R).

The Democrat led De La Cruz by nearly 14 percentage points — 56.9 to 43.2 percent — with 52 percent of the vote reported by DDHQ as of 12:34 a.m. Wednesday.

The Democrat campaigned on lowering rising costs of living in the state, preventing lawmakers from trading stocks, expanding access to affordable housing, securing the southern border and restricting new data center developments in the state.

He was supported by Casar, Rep. Joaquin Castro (D-Texas) and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg (D).

Garcia has repeatedly criticized the Trump administration’s military operations against Iran and the deaths of service members during this conflict and resulting rise in fuel and living costs.

“No more endless wars,” he wrote in a social media post at the end of August. “I’m running because our troops and their families deserve better.”

articles.title: Republican reckoning: Accountability finally comes for Trump
articles.summary: All the ad spending in the world didn’t convince voters that Republicans had even the concepts of a plan for fixing Donald Trump’s worsening economic mess.
articles.body:
Ad spending on this year’s midterm elections clocked in at more than $11.21 billion , an eye-watering number that even edges past the $11.2 billion spent during the 2024 presidential cycle. All that money went to perpetuate the wall of noise marketing a campaign cycle that felt like it would never end. From sponsored Facebook posts to YouTube ads and television spots to good old billboards, the 2026 midterms ought to be known as the election cycle no one could escape.

Yet all the ad spending in the world didn’t convince voters that Republicans had even the concepts of a plan for fixing Donald Trump’s worsening economic mess.

The party limped into this year’s midterms carrying the burden of a historically unpopular president and a historically bad affordability crisis . It stumbled over the finish line in a state of total exhaustion, successful only in its mission to alienate nearly every voting bloc it gained in 2024.

One has to wonder if some of the Republicans who lost their seats were just glad that this whole disgraceful march was finally over.

By midnight it was clear that the long-predicted Democratic wave wasn’t just a mirage of polling or a conspiracy of the anti-Trump media. Democrats notched high-profile Senate wins in Kansas, Iowa, Texas, Ohio, South Carolina and North Carolina, many by convincing margins. In Texas, James Talarico romped to victory over Donald Trump’s hand-picked nominee, Ken Paxton, by nearly 20 points.

Democrats also made major inroads into a Deep South that Republicans once proudly called their “ red wall, ” flipping governor’s mansions in Texas and Georgia. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black female governor of a state that was once the heart of the Confederacy.

The scale and size of Democrats’ triumph was so great that even Trump seemed to realize it would be pointless to rehash his perennial claims of election fraud. Instead, Trump sheepishly told The New York Times that he would accept the election results as legitimate. “We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out,” Trump said.

I guess there are some drubbings so brutal that even MAGA is forced to accept reality.

The specter of Tuesday’s outcome also appeared to send deep cracks through the MAGA movement as Republicans came to grips with Trump’s rapidly declining political clout. A day before voters headed to the polls, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) publicly broke with the president on issues ranging from the Iran War to immigration enforcement. Meanwhile, longtime Trump allies, including seven-term Rep. Scott Perry (R-Pa.), lost their seats.

Trump now heads into 2027 with fewer friends than ever on Capitol Hill and a Republican Party that is deeply skeptical of his value as a messenger. It’s arguably the weakest Trump has been since the immediate aftermath of the January 6 Capitol attack . After years spent defying political gravity, Tuesday’s sweeping rebuke now has Trump looking and feeling like a lame-duck president.

The same can’t be said for Democrats. Yesterday’s results were a stunning vindication for a Democratic Party that emerged from its 2024 loss to Trump both emotionally and organizationally shattered. Bolstered by Trump’s historic economic and foreign policy failures, Democrats managed to mend most of their public divisions while crafting a message that appealed to the Latinos, Arab Americans, young people and independent voters who abandoned them two years ago.

Democrats’ message was as simple as it was effective: Trump is making you poorer .

The affordability crisis became the unifying message of progressives and centrists, establishment Dems and outsider insurgents alike, and the party’s willingness to engage with voters’ frustrations opened doors with rural voters and traditional conservatives long thought to be beyond the reach of Democratic economic appeals. The party’s affordability campaign asked those voters to choose between a plan they might not completely agree with and Trump’s lack of any plan at all.

On Tuesday, Associated Press exit polling showed that affordability concerns and public corruption ranked near the top of voters’ concerns, while a supermajority of Americans blamed Trump for making their lives worse. If anything, those numbers understated just how angry voters were at Republicans who promised them a Golden Age only to deliver higher prices and a total lack of accountability.

Republicans don’t have any more answers to those crises today than they did a month or a year ago. Now they can add massive voter disillusionment and a demoralized party base to their mounting problems. The Republican Party is the weakest it’s been since the Bush administration collapsed under the pressure of the 2008 financial crisis, yet it is still bound to a president who can’t — or won’t — acknowledge his own staggering unpopularity. Republicans may finally be thinking of a future beyond Trump, but actually ridding themselves of a man who never surrenders the spotlight will be another headache entirely.

Max Burns is a veteran Democratic strategist and founder of Third Degree Strategies.

articles.title: Kingston wins Georgia House seat left open by Carter
articles.summary: Republican Jim Kingston, the son of former Rep. Jack Kingston (R-Ga.), is projected to win Georgia’s 1st Congressional District, defeating Democrat Amanda Hollowell, according to Decision Desk HQ. Kingston will succeed Rep. Buddy Carter (R-Ga.), who gave up his seat to launch a costly yet unsuccessful bid for Senate, where he finished third in the…
articles.body:
Republican Jim Kingston, the son of former Rep. Jack Kingston (R-Ga.), is projected to win Georgia’s 1st Congressional District, defeating Democrat Amanda Hollowell, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Kingston will succeed Rep. Buddy Carter (R-Ga.), who gave up his seat to launch a costly yet unsuccessful bid for Senate , where he finished third in the Republican runoff. Kingston’s father represented the same coastal Georgia district for more than two decades, from 1993 to 2015.

The Republican is projected to eke out a win over the Democrat — 50.7 percent to 49.31 — in the solid red district, per DDHQ.

The district, which includes Savannah and much of Georgia’s southern coast, has remained firmly in Republican hands for decades. President Trump, who endorsed Kingston ahead of the primary, carried the district by nearly 16 percentage points in 2025, while Carter won reelection that year by 24 points.

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report had rated the district as “solid Republican,” making Kingston the favorite heading into the general election.

He won a crowded six-way Republican primary in May with just a little more than 52 percent of the vote, clearing the majority needed to avoid a runoff. His opponents included Pat Farrell, Kandiss Taylor and Brian Montgomery.

Trump described Kingston as a successful businessperson while praising his family’s support of the MAGA movement.

Kingston, 35, is a Savannah native and political newcomer who spent his professional career in the insurance industry, most recently serving as senior vice president at Marsh McLennan. He attended the University of Georgia from 2009 to 2013 but left before completing his degree to begin working full-time.

Kingston faced criticism from some of his Republican primary opponents over his lack of political experience and ties to his father, who became a lobbyist in Washington after leaving Congress.

The Republican campaigned on strengthening border security, cutting federal spending and regulations, protecting Georgia’s agricultural industry and expanding domestic energy production. He also called for lowering taxes and supporting immigration enforcement agencies.

Hollowell, a political strategist and community organizer, secured the Democratic nomination after defeating Joyce Marie Griggs in a June runoff. The Democrat serves as chief of campaigns at Color of Change, a national racial justice organization, and previously worked on voting rights and economic justice initiatives, including with former first lady Michelle Obama’s organization When We All Vote.

articles.title: The blue wave that broke Trump’s Republican map
articles.summary: Democrats soared to victory Tuesday night across races for Congress and governors’ mansions, and are set to retake power in Congress by higher margins than the party has had since last century. It’s a striking condemnation from voters of the war in Iran and President Trump’s leadership of the Republican Party. Midterm elections are usually…
articles.body:
Democrats soared to victory Tuesday night across races for Congress and governors’ mansions, and are set to retake power in Congress by higher margins than the party has had since last century.

It’s a striking condemnation from voters of the war in Iran and President Trump’s leadership of the Republican Party.

Midterm elections are usually a referendum on the party in power, and often result in at least one chamber of Congress flipping. But this “blue wave” goes even further, delivering at least 6 seats in the Senate and at least 24 in the House.

Democrats also swept statewide races, flipping at least 4 governorships.

In the House, the party is likely to have a majority as large as 254 seats, big enough to allow for defections, a cushion Republicans did not enjoy over the last two years.

Democratic leaders, predictably, are doing victory laps and planning their next moves.

“There is now a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America now and on into the future,” said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on Tuesday night. “Americans voted for change, and now Democrats must deliver.”

“MAGA extremists are on the run from sea to shining sea,” said Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is likely to be the next Speaker of the House.

Republicans, meanwhile, are licking their wounds. The party will likely head into a scattered season of figuring out what the best way forward will be as the 2028 presidential race begins – without Trump.

“Trump’s iron grip on the Republican Party is a melting ice cube,” said Dan Eberhart, a Republican donor.

Texas-based Republican strategist Brendan Steinhauser dubbed the night an “utter disaster” in a text message to The Hill, including a gif of the Titanic sinking.

Some Republicans are already pointing the finger at Trump: his handling of the war in Iran and his attempt at kingmaking candidates like Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, against the party’s wishes, who ultimately lost.

“Iran War 100 percent. Corruption 100 percent. Bad candidates 100 percent. One common denominator for them all…Trump,” one Republican strategist told The Hill.

Trump laid blame on his absence from the ballot, arguing that he would have won in a landslide if he was up for election himself. The president also notably lashed out at Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R ), who lost his reelection bid, after the governor noticeably stayed far away from Trump on the campaign trail.

“Tonight is further proof that Republican candidates can’t take turnout for granted when President Trump isn’t on the ballot,” one Trump world source told The Hill.

“Democrats are renting many of these seats, and the independents who voted for them will swing back hard after two years of a socialist majority and a serious case of buyer’s remorse,” the source added.

Trump made himself a centerpiece of the Republican campaign effort, urging voters to “pretend” he was on the ballot. Republicans argued that deploying Trump on the campaign trail would help the party replicate its 2024 turnout, but the strategy had the opposite effect.

“It’s a rejection of Trump’s rallies and closing arguments. His coattails were not long enough,” Eberhart said.

Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah), in a Substack essay published Tuesday night, encouraged Republicans to learn from this election and return to the roots of the party, which he described as “limited government, free trade, resolute diplomacy and global leadership, and fiscal responsibility.”

“Unfortunately, by putting aside our core values, we’ve let down a lot of those same Americans who recently joined our party,” Curtis wrote. “Instead of finally seeing relief on prices after the reckless Biden years, they saw a hastily planned war disrupt oil markets. Instead of enjoying a restoration of order and integrity in our government, they read headline after headline of scandals, incompetence, and corruption. Instead of economic stability and fiscal prudence, they saw the public debt balloon past $40 trillion—leading to volatile markets. Instead of peace through strength, they saw the leader of the free world side with Putin over a strategic ally.”

Curtis, who was elected last year, could be a thought leader in the Republicans’ next chapter of redefinition.

Democrats’ wins in specific races also pointed to those issues where Trump and Republicans by extension were losing ground quickly with voters.

In Kansas, Democrats were bullish in recent months as voters grew more disenchanted with immigration enforcement raids that affected the meatpacking industry; with diesel and gas prices and with the economic effects of tariffs. Those voters sent a Democrat to the Senate for the first time in nearly a century.

In Iowa, too, voters pushed back on mainstream Trump-backed candidates for Senate and governor. Tariffs and agricultural impacts of the war have hit Iowa hard, and the state’s high cancer rate put health care and environmental policy in a central spotlight that favored Democratic platforms. In Ohio’s Senate race, some gubernatorial races and many House races around the country, Democratic candidates seized the upper hand on regulating data centers and pushing back on the tech industry.

As they take stock of what voters don’t want, Democrats are also looking ahead to what the cushy majority will allow them to do. Ending the Iran war has been a central focus for Democrats’ 2027 wishlists, and with a broad majority in both chambers, they will have more leeway to choke off funding or otherwise compel the administration to end the conflict.

The midterms could also be a referendum on Trump and congressional Republicans’ signature legislation, the “One, Big, Beautiful Bill” signed into law last year that cut some taxes and caused many Americans to lose Medicaid benefits. This has also been a key fixture of Democratic attack ads, and leaders have signaled they’re eager to jump into restoring health care benefits and further strengthening the federal safety net.

The main legislative goals Democrats have outlined have to do with their central campaign trail word: “affordability.” That could mean specific legislation designed to cut costs, but Schumer suggested it could also mean investigations into the administration.

“Our number one focus has to be producing for the American people in terms of their number one need, the high costs that Trump has imposed on them,” Schumer said. “And second, to go after the corruption. This is the most corrupt administration in American history.”

Oversight has been a chief topic: Jeffries and his leadership will be empowered to carry out investigations against Trump administration officials and even pursue impeachment proceedings, although some Democrats have cautioned against leaning too hard.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the likely next Chairman of the House Committee on Oversight, summed his intentions up in a post on X: “LAWYER UP.”

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), likely top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, which oversees tax policy, just said : “Subpoenas.” Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) replied in a similar vein to a post on X suggesting “live televised trials of Big Tech executives.”

Trump appeared to offer a conciliatory tone in an interview on Fox News just after midnight, going as far as to compliment Democrats on their work in the election.

“I think the Democrats did a good job. I really do. I think they did a good job. They fought hard,” he said.

The president also did not rule out working with Democrats in Congress on issues including immigration.

“I’m a person who likes getting things done,” Trump said, noting he and Republicans can’t work with Democrats on everything.

“But I can work with them on a lot of things. I mean, we can work with them on immigration. I think immigration is a big deal,” he said.

articles.title: Bo French loses TX Railroad Commissioner race

The Republican lost support from several prominent Republicans in his state after he posted on social media about University of Texas at Austin students of South Asian descent. In a…
articles.body:
Bo French, the GOP nominee running for Texas railroad commissioner, is projected to lose his race to Democrat Jon Rosenthal, according to Decision Desk HQ .

The Republican lost support from several prominent Republicans in his state after he posted on social media about University of Texas at Austin students of South Asian descent.

In a September social media post , the candidate reshared an image of South Asian students attending a Texas football game.

“I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined,” French wrote in the post’s caption.

Outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn (R) announced in September he would not cast a vote for French in this race, warning that French could “drag the whole ticket down because of his racist comments.”

Karl Rove, who served as a top political adviser for former President George W. Bush, also stated he would not support French and said he would vote for Rosenthal instead .

Rosenthal is a mechanical engineer and a four-term member of the Texas House.

French’s loss follows a shocking upset for Republicans in the Texas Senate race, in which Democratic state Rep. James Talarico flipped the seat for his party.

articles.title: Hatcher wins Tennessee House race after defeating Ogles in GOP primary
articles.summary: Former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher is projected to win Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District over his opponents Democrat Chaz Molder, independent James Johnson and independent Micheál O’Leary, according to Decision Desk HQ. The win comes after Hatcher defeated Trump-backed Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) in the GOP primary. The seat has been held by the GOP…
articles.body:
Former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher is projected to win Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District over his opponents Democrat Chaz Molder, independent James Johnson and independent Micheál O’Leary, according to Decision Desk HQ .

The win comes after Hatcher defeated Trump-backed Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) in the GOP primary. The seat has been held by the GOP since Ogles flipped the seat from Democrats in 2022.

President Trump switched his endorsement to Hatcher following his win over Ogles, writing on Truth Social, “Good luck Charlie! Run tough and hard. You have my Complete and Total Endorsement!”

Hatcher writes on his campaign website that his positions are “pro-Gun. Pro-Life. Pro-Trump. Farm Strong.”

The race was favored for the GOP as the 5th Congressional District was majorly redrawn in a rare mid-decade redistricting effort — excluding all parts of Nashville. The area is one Ogles lost in 2024 by over 20,000 votes, according to DDHQ .

At a public forum against Molder, Hatcher identified that his top priority was to tackle the cost of living. The Democrat attacked Hatcher on Trump’s international tariffs, which are projected to hit Tennessee hard.

Hatcher defended the strategic use of tariffs, arguing that they are “a tool; they can be used effectively, sometimes badly,” according to the Nashville Banner .

“We need to support American industries, and we need to support American agriculture so that we can … not have other countries hold us hostage,” he continued, pointing to agriculture and steel as examples of industries where he believes tariffs can be used to support American producers.

Hatcher stated at the forum that he had the occasional disagreement with Trump, particularly the president’s plan to import beef. The plan would import 300,000 metric tons of beef without tariffs for 90 days from Brazil and Argentina at 25 percent below current market prices.

articles.title: Garrett clinches Rose’s open House seat in Tennessee
articles.summary: Republican Johnny Garrett is projected to clinch the Tennessee House seat left open by outgoing Rep. John Rose (R-Tenn.), defeating Democrat Mike Croley, Independent Christopher Monday and Independent Angus Purdy, according to The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). Garrett, a self-described “Trump Conservative,” previously served as the state House’s majority whip since 2019 before…
articles.body:
Republican Johnny Garrett is projected to clinch the Tennessee House seat left open by outgoing Rep. John Rose (R-Tenn.), defeating Democrat Mike Croley, Independent Christopher Monday and Independent Angus Purdy, according to The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

Garrett, a self-described “Trump Conservative,” previously served as the state House’s majority whip since 2019 before running for Tennessee’s 6th Congressional District seat.

While in the state legislature, Garrett sponsored bills that would have narrowed who can run in primaries for federal office in Tennessee — excluding those not born in the U.S. or have dual citizenship. This was quashed before it could be debated.

In an interview with WKRN News 2 , Garrett said the legislation was necessary because “look at what Congresswoman Omar Ilmar has done in Minnesota.”

“We cannot let and ever let Tennessee and Nashville become Minneapolis or Minnesota,” he added.

Another proposed bill that Garrett sponsored would require Tennessee law enforcement to enter deals with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Law enforcement that failed to comply were threatened with losing state funding from grants and contracts.

Garrett campaigned for fighting against inflation , deporting people who entered the country illegally and keeping men out of women’s sports.

Rose announced he would not be running for reelection and instead unveiled a bid for Tennessee’s open gubernatorial seat.
